questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four criteria this lesson sets for choosing the project's dataset?
options: The dataset must be synthetic and specifically generated to favor the quantum classifier
Few features (roughly 2-4), fitting a small qubit budget under angle encoding
Binary or small number of classes, matching the single-qubit measurement classifier structure
Real, publicly available, and well-documented, so a classical baseline comparison is meaningful
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly requires a REAL, publicly documented dataset -- a synthetic dataset invented to flatter one method would be exactly the kind of cherry-picking Lesson 4 warned against, not a valid criterion.

questions.q: For the Iris dataset reduced to 2 features (petal length, petal width) and 2 classes, how many qubits does angle encoding need?
options: 2 qubits -- one rotation per feature
4 qubits, one for each original Iris feature
13 qubits, matching the Wine dataset's feature count
0 qubits, since Iris is a classical-only dataset
questions.explain: Angle encoding needs one qubit per feature, so a 2-feature reduction of Iris needs exactly 2 qubits -- comfortably within simulator range and far from barren-plateau territory.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that using a classic, well-studied benchmark dataset (like Iris) is the RIGHT choice for this project, not a cop-out?
options: A well-characterized dataset lets the classical baseline comparison in Lesson 25 compare against results the field already understands well, satisfying the fair-comparison standard from Lesson 4
Classic datasets are quantum-native and were specifically designed for quantum classifiers
Novel datasets are always too small to be used in any machine learning project
Classic benchmark datasets guarantee the quantum classifier will outperform classical baselines
questions.explain: Using a well-documented dataset that's already used in PennyLane/Qiskit ML's own tutorials means results are comparable to publicly known outputs, directly supporting a fair, well-documented benchmark comparison rather than undermining the project's rigor.

questions.q: What does 'real dataset' specifically mean in this lesson's framing?
options: Collected from actual physical measurements, publicly documented with known characteristics, and used elsewhere in the field for comparability -- not invented numbers chosen to flatter a method
Any dataset generated by a random number generator counts as real as long as it has the right number of features
Only datasets collected after the year 2020 count as real for this project
A dataset is real only if it was specifically created for quantum computing research
questions.explain: The lesson ties 'real' to actual physical measurement, public documentation, and field-wide comparability -- exactly the properties that make a benchmark comparison meaningful rather than fabricated.

questions.q: Why would a brand-new, never-before-studied dataset make Lesson 25's 'fair comparison' standard HARDER to satisfy for this project?
options: There would be no existing, independently-verified classical baseline results to compare against, and no way to sanity-check whether the comparison itself was set up fairly
Brand-new datasets are always too large to fit any qubit budget
Brand-new datasets cannot be loaded into PennyLane or Qiskit Machine Learning
There is no actual difficulty; a brand-new dataset would make the comparison easier, not harder
questions.explain: A novel dataset has no established classical-method track record to compare against and no way to sanity-check the setup against known tutorial or published results -- exactly why classic benchmarks better serve the fair-comparison goal here.
